# Week 1 - Day 4 - Fundamentals - Codegen and finding your way around locators

By the end of this lesson you will know what Codegen and the Inspector actually do, why
they reach for `getByRole`/`getByPlaceholder` over old id/xpath/css locators, and why a spec
file's name isn't just cosmetic.

> **No new TypeScript today** — locator strings and file naming aren't new language syntax,
> so there's no Day 4.1. [Day 2](/learn/w1/d2/p2) and [Day 3](/learn/w1/d3/p2) got you set up
> and running; today is about *finding* what to put inside a test.

> **Try it here**, plus one run-it-yourself step.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You'll use** | `getByRole` · `getByPlaceholder` · Codegen and the Inspector |
| **On** | the course's banking app, signed in as Leela |
| **Run it yourself** | Codegen opens two real windows — there is no way to fake that in a lesson cell |
| **The idea to take away** | locate by what an element *is* to a user, not by where it sits in the markup |

## Codegen — run this yourself, in a real terminal

```bash
npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/
```

This opens **two windows**: a real browser you click around in, and the **Inspector**, which
turns every click/type/navigate into generated TypeScript locator code live, as you do it.

**This is genuinely run-it-yourself, like `page.pause()` elsewhere in this course** — there's
no way to fake a transcript of "what Codegen would produce" in a lesson cell and have it
mean anything. Open a terminal, run the command above, log in as Leela
(`leela@gmail.com` / `Leela@123`), and watch the panel on the right fill in. Close both
windows when you're done; it doesn't save anything until you copy code out of it yourself.

## What Codegen reaches for, and why

Codegen doesn't just grab *any* selector that happens to work — it's built to prefer
locators a redesign is less likely to break.

| Strategy | Example | Survives a redesign? |
|---|---|---|
| `id` / `class` from generated CSS | `#ng-x7f2q3` | Often not — build tools regenerate these |
| Raw XPath | `//div[3]/button[1]` | No — breaks the moment the layout shifts |
| `getByRole` | `page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" })` | Yes — tied to what the element *is* and its accessible name |
| `getByPlaceholder` | `page.getByPlaceholder("Enter Email")` | Yes — tied to user-facing text, not markup structure |

`getByRole`/`getByLabel`/`getByPlaceholder`/`getByText` are all built around what a screen
reader (or a human) would use to find the element — which is far more stable than internal
markup, and is exactly why Codegen defaults to them.

## Example — the locators Codegen would hand you for this login form

**Objective:** use the same kind of role/placeholder-based locators Codegen produces, against
the real login form.

Line by line:

| Line | What it does |
|---|---|
| `page.getByPlaceholder("Enter Email")` | Finds the field by its placeholder text — same as Codegen would generate for it |
| `page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" })` | Finds the button by its accessible role + visible label |
| `page.waitForURL("**/dashboard")` | Waits for the post-login redirect, proving the click actually worked |

**Expected result:** a screenshot of the dashboard, signed in as Leela.

**Challenge:** swap in Katy's credentials from `USERS[1]` and confirm it still works — same
locators, different data.

blocks.text:
## Why the `.spec.ts` suffix isn't cosmetic

Playwright's `testMatch` (which you read in this repo's config on Day 2.2) only picks up
files ending in `.spec.ts` (or `.test.ts`). A file named `login.ts` sitting right next to
`login.spec.ts` is **invisible** to the test runner — not broken, not skipped, just never
looked at. [Day 4.3](/learn/w1/d4/p3) proves this for real rather than asking you to trust it.

## Folder organization

Day 2.3 introduced splitting test folders by type (`UI_test`/`API_test`) instead of one flat
`tests/` folder. The same principle applies to `testDir`: whatever convention you pick, the
test runner only needs `testMatch` to find the `.spec.ts` files inside it — organize
sub-folders however makes sense for your team (by feature, by test type, by app area).

## Best practices - Prefer `getByRole`/`getByLabel`/`getByPlaceholder`/`getByText` over `id`/class/xpath — let Codegen's defaults be your defaults too. - Use Codegen to get a **first draft**, then clean it up — it records everything you clicked, including accidental clicks. - Always name generated specs `*.spec.ts` — a missing suffix is a silent, not a loud, failure. ## Common mistakes | Mistake | What you see | Fix | |---|---|---| | Wrote a spec file without the `.spec.ts` suffix | `npx playwright test` runs, reports 0 tests changed — the file is just silently absent | Rename it to end in `.spec.ts` | | Copied Codegen's raw output verbatim into the suite | Works, but full of one-off clicks and no structure | Treat it as a draft — extract the locators, drop the noise | | Reached for `getByRole("link", ...)` on this app's dashboard | Finds nothing | This app's dashboard tiles are `

` elements, not `` — noted in `_shared/CONCEPTS.md` |
Why does Codegen generate `getByRole("button", { name: "Login" })` rather than something like `#ng-x7f2q3`?

options: Because role locators are faster to evaluate
Because it is tied to what the element is and what it says, which a redesign is far less likely to change
Because generated ids are not unique enough to match one element
checkpoint.explanation: A build tool regenerates `#ng-x7f2q3` on the next deploy and an XPath breaks the moment the layout shifts. Role, label, placeholder and text are what a screen reader or a human uses to find something, and that survives the markup being rewritten underneath it.

blocks.text: You save a test as `login.ts` instead of `login.spec.ts`. What happens when you run the suite?

options: It fails with an error about the file name
It is skipped, and reported as skipped
Nothing at all — the file is never looked at, with no error and no warning
checkpoint.explanation: `testMatch` only collects `.spec.ts` (or `.test.ts`). The file sits there, valid and completely invisible. That silence is the danger: a loud failure gets fixed in a minute, and this one can hide a whole test file for weeks. [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3) proves it rather than asking you to take it on trust.

blocks.text: How should you treat the code Codegen hands you?

options: As a first draft — take the locators, drop the accidental clicks it also recorded
As finished code, since it only generates stable locators
As reference only; retyping it by hand is the point
checkpoint.explanation: Codegen records everything you did, including the clicks you did not mean. Its value is the locators it chose for you; the structure around them is yours to write. Pasting a raw recording into a suite is how you end up with tests nobody can read.

blocks.text:
- Prefer `getByRole` / `getByLabel` / `getByPlaceholder` / `getByText`. Let Codegen's defaults be yours. - Generated ids and raw XPath encode the markup of the day, and break when it changes. - Codegen gives a **draft**: keep the locators, drop the noise. - **A missing `.spec.ts` suffix is a silent failure, not a loud one** — the runner simply never looks at the file. - On this app the dashboard tiles are `

` elements, so `getByRole("link", ...)` finds nothing.

## What's next

[Day 4.3](/learn/w1/d4/p3) proves the naming-convention rule above for real, by writing a file
without the suffix and watching Playwright ignore it.

# Week 1 - Day 4 - Implementation - Proving the `.spec.ts` naming convention

By the end of this lesson you will have watched Playwright genuinely ignore a test file
because of its name, then watched the same file get picked up the moment you rename it.

> **No new API here either** — this slot is normally "the same API, inside a framework", but
> there's no framework yet. Today it's the same locators from Day 4.2, used to prove a rule
> about *discovery* rather than to teach a new call.

| | |
|---|---|
| **New API** | none — the same locators from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2), used to prove a rule about discovery |
| **What you'll watch** | a valid test file ignored entirely, then found, purely because of its name |
| **The tool** | `npx playwright test <dir> --list` — counts what the runner can actually see |

**Expected result:** the listing shows `day3-smoke.spec.ts`'s two tests and **nothing from

Playwright code in it, and is completely invisible to the runner. No error, no warning — this
is the "silent, not loud" failure mode worth remembering.

blocks.text: ## Step 3 — rename it, and watch it appear

**Expected result:** now `Total: 3 tests in 2 files` — the exact same code, now discovered,
purely because of the `.spec.ts` suffix.

**Challenge:** delete `week1/generated/day4-renamed.spec.ts` and re-run the listing to confirm
it drops back to 2 tests, 1 file.

## What a reviewer would look for

- A generated spec file that always ends in `.spec.ts` — never `.ts`, never `.test.js`.
- No silent assumption that "the file is there so it must be running" — when in doubt,
  `--list` and count.
`--list` reports `Total: 2 tests in 1 file`, but you know there are two test files in that folder. What does that tell you?

options: One file failed to compile and was skipped
One file is not being collected at all — almost always the `.spec.ts` suffix
The second file's tests are marked `.skip`
checkpoint.explanation: A compile error is loud and a `.skip` still appears in the listing as skipped. A file the pattern never matched contributes nothing — no line, no warning, no count. Run `--list` whenever a file's tests seem to have vanished.

blocks.text: Renaming `day4-not-a-spec.ts` to `day4-renamed.spec.ts` took the listing from 2 tests to 3. What changed inside the file?

options: Nothing — the same code, now discovered purely because of the name
The rename triggered a recompile that fixed an import
The test was registered with the runner as part of the rename
checkpoint.explanation: Not one character of the code changed. Discovery is a filename question, decided by `testMatch` before any of your code is read. There is no registration step anywhere in Playwright — which is convenient right up until a name is wrong.

blocks.text:
- Discovery happens by **filename**, before a line of your code is read.
- A file that does not match is invisible: no error, no warning, no count.
- `npx playwright test <dir> --list` is the cheap way to check what the runner can actually see.
- Never assume "the file is there, so it must be running" — when in doubt, list and count.

## When you're done

You can now find good locators and understand why Playwright discovers (or ignores) a file.
[Day 5](/learn/w1/d5/p1) is the week's capstone — your first real test, and the lesson about
assertions that makes the rest of this course make sense.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Run `npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`
yourself. After logging in, click through to the **Payments** tile. Copy the locator(s)
Codegen generated for that click into a comment in the cell below.

**Where.** Your terminal for Codegen itself; a cell here for the locator you copied.

**How you'll know it worked.** You have a real `getByRole` or `getByText` line copied out of

problems.solution:
**Run Codegen from your own terminal** — it opens a real browser window alongside the Inspector, which the studio's Run button cannot do.

```bash
npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/
```

Log in, then click the **Payments** tile. Codegen writes something close to:

```ts
await page.getByPlaceholder('Enter Email').fill('leela@gmail.com');
await page.getByPlaceholder('Enter Password').fill('Leela@123');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' }).click();
await page.getByText('Payments').click();
```

**Two things worth noticing in what it produced.**

It reached for `getByPlaceholder` and `getByRole` before anything else — Codegen prefers locators a human can read, and falls back to CSS only when nothing better exists. And **it recorded no assertion.** Every line is an action. Codegen watches what you *do*; it has no way to know what you *expect*, which is the gap Day 5.2 makes painfully concrete.

> Treat Codegen output as a first draft. It is excellent at telling you what a control is called and poor at deciding what matters.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Day 4.2 contrasted `getByRole`/`getByPlaceholder` with old id/xpath/css
locators. Write two or three sentences explaining *why* the role/placeholder version is more
likely to survive a redesign — be specific about what changes in a typical redesign (CSS
classes, DOM nesting, generated ids) and why each locator style is or isn't affected by that
change.

**Where.** A cell here, as a comment.

**How you'll know it worked.** Your explanation names a concrete kind of change (e.g. "a
build tool regenerates class names on every deploy") rather than staying abstract.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.**

> A redesign usually changes three things: the CSS classes (a new design system, or a utility-class refactor), the DOM nesting (a wrapper `<div>` added for layout, a component split in two), and any generated ids (`ctl00_MainContent_btn3` becomes `ctl00_MainContent_btn7` because a control was inserted above it).
>
> **A CSS-class locator** breaks on the first of those. `.btn-primary-lg` is a *styling* decision, and styling is exactly what a redesign exists to change.
>
> **An XPath path** breaks on the second. `//div[2]/form/div[3]/input` encodes the shape of the tree; one wrapper div and it points somewhere else — or worse, at a different control that happens to sit in that position now.
>
> **A generated id** breaks on the third, and breaks silently.
>
> **`getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })`** survives all three, because none of them change what the control *is* or what it *says*. The button is still a button and still reads "Login" — that is the contract with the user, and a redesign that breaks it has changed the product, not the markup.

**The underlying rule:** anchor on what the user perceives — role, label, placeholder, visible text — not on how the page is built. The exception is a genuinely stable, purpose-built hook such as `data-testid`, which the team agrees not to change.
